children.label: a
children.prompt: Same nursery as above. Find the probability that exactly 4 lavender plants and exactly 2 rosemary plants survive.

answer.worked:
$X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(6,0.8)$ and $Y\sim\operatorname{Bin}(4,0.6)$.
$$\begin{align*}P(X=4)&=\binom64(0.8)^4(0.2)^2=0.24576\\P(Y=2)&=\binom42(0.6)^2(0.4)^2=0.3456\\P(X=4\text{ and }Y=2)&=0.24576\times0.3456\\&\approx0.0849\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: A farm has 7 hens and 5 ducks. Each hen lays an egg on a given day with probability 0.7 and each duck with probability 0.5, independently. Find the probability that exactly 5 hens and exactly 1 duck lay an egg.

answer.worked:
Let $X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(7,0.7)$ count hens and $Y\sim\operatorname{Bin}(5,0.5)$ count ducks.
$$\begin{align*}P(X=5)&=\binom75(0.7)^5(0.3)^2=0.3176523\\P(Y=1)&=\binom51(0.5)^1(0.5)^4=0.15625\\P(X=5\text{ and }Y=1)&=0.3176523\times0.15625\\&\approx0.0496\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: A fruit box has 3 mangoes and 2 peaches. Each mango is ripe with probability 0.6 and each peach with probability 0.5, independently. Find the probability that exactly 2 pieces of fruit in total are ripe.

answer.worked:
Let $X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(3,0.6)$ count ripe mangoes and $Y\sim\operatorname{Bin}(2,0.5)$ count ripe peaches. Two ripe in total can happen in three ways: $(X,Y)=(2,0),(1,1),(0,2)$.
$$\begin{align*}P(X=2)P(Y=0)&=0.432\times0.25=0.108\\P(X=1)P(Y=1)&=0.288\times0.5=0.144\\P(X=0)P(Y=2)&=0.064\times0.25=0.016\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}P(\text{2 ripe in total})&=0.108+0.144+0.016\\&=0.2680\end{align*}$$

answer.short: Choosing the 2 successes determines the 4 failures, so the counts are equal.
answer.worked: Every choice of 2 successful trials from the 6 leaves exactly 4 failed trials. Conversely, choosing the 4 failed trials determines the 2 successful trials. Thus both combinations count the same arrangements.

answer.short: Success and failure have different probabilities, so arrangements with 2 successes and with 4 successes have different probabilities.

children.prompt: If six dice are rolled one hundred times, how many times would you expect the number of even numbers showing to exceed the number of odd numbers showing? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

content.prompt: It is known that 15% of a large constituency voted for the Working Together Party at the last election. A poll of 100 people is taken and they are asked whether they voted WTP.

children.prompt: What is the mean and standard deviation for this poll? Give the standard deviation correct to 2 decimal places.

answer.worked:
Let $X$ be the number of WTP voters in the poll. Then $X\sim B(100,0.15)$.
$$\begin{aligned}\mu&=np=100(0.15)=15\\\sigma&=\sqrt{np(1-p)}=\sqrt{100(0.15)(0.85)}=\sqrt{12.75}\approx3.57\end{aligned}$$

children.prompt: What is the probability that in the sample, the number of WTP voters lies within half a standard deviation of the mean? Give your answer correct to 3 decimal places.

answer.worked:

Its endpoints are approximately 13.215 and 16.785, so the possible integer values are 14, 15 and 16.
$$\begin{aligned}P(14\le X\le16)&=\sum_{x=14}^{16}\binom{100}{x}(0.15)^x(0.85)^{100-x}\\&\approx0.325\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt:
$\textbf{(i)}$ Explain why the probability of getting a sum of 5 when one pair of fair dice is tossed is $\frac{1}{9}$.

$\textbf{(ii)}$ Find the probability of getting a sum of 5 at least twice when a pair of dice is tossed 7 times.

answer.worked:
$\textbf{(i)}$
When a pair of fair dice is tossed, the total number of possible outcomes is $6 \times 6 = 36$.
The outcomes that yield a sum of 5 are $(1, 4), (2, 3), (3, 2), (4, 1)$.
There are 4 favourable outcomes.
$$\begin{align*}
\text{Probability} &= \frac{4}{36} \\
&= \frac{1}{9}
\end{align*}$$

$\textbf{(ii)}$
Let $X$ be the number of times a sum of 5 occurs in 7 tosses. This follows a binomial distribution with $n=7$ and $p = \frac{1}{9}$.
We need to find $P(X \ge 2)$, which is the complement of $P(X < 2)$.
$$\begin{align*}
P(X \ge 2) &= 1 - P(X < 2) \\
&= 1 - (P(X=0) + P(X=1)) \\
P(X = 0) &= \binom{7}{0} \left(\frac{1}{9}\right)^0 \left(\frac{8}{9}\right)^7 = \left(\frac{8}{9}\right)^7 \\
P(X = 1) &= \binom{7}{1} \left(\frac{1}{9}\right)^1 \left(\frac{8}{9}\right)^6 = 7 \times \frac{8^6}{9^7} \\
P(X \ge 2) &= 1 - \left( \frac{8^7}{9^7} + \frac{7 \times 8^6}{9^7} \right) \\
&= 1 - \frac{8^7 + 7 \times 8^6}{9^7} \\
&\approx 0.1779 \quad \text{(to 4 d.p.)}
\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
Consider a random variable $X$ which follows a binomial distribution with parameters $n$ and $p$, where $n$ is the number of independent trials and $p$ is the probability of success with $0<p<1$.
Given $\frac{P(X=r)}{P(X=n-r)}$ is independent of $n$ and $r$.
What is the value of $p$?

$\text{A. } \frac{1}{2}$
$\text{B. } \frac{1}{3}$
$\text{C. } \frac{1}{4}$
$\text{D. } \frac{3}{4}$

answer.short: A. $p=\frac12$. Use $\binom nr=\binom n{n-r}$ to cancel the binomial coefficients.
answer.worked:
Let $q=1-p$. For $X\sim \operatorname{Bin}(n,p)$:
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{P(X=r)}{P(X=n-r)} &= \frac{\binom{n}{r}p^r q^{n-r}}{\binom{n}{n-r}p^{n-r}q^r} \\
&= \frac{p^r q^{n-r}}{p^{n-r}q^r} \\
&= \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{n-2r}
\end{align*}$$
For this to be independent of $n$ and $r$, the base must be $1$:
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{q}{p} &= 1 \\
q &= p \\
1-p &= p \\
p &= \frac{1}{2}
\end{align*}$$
Correct answer: A.

content.prompt:
In an endurance event, the probability that a competitor will complete the course is $p$ and the probability that a competitor will not complete the course is $q = 1 - p$.
Teams consist of either two or four competitors.
A team scores points if at least half its members complete the course.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the probability that a four-member team will have at least three of its members not complete the course is $4pq^3 + q^4$.

answer.worked:
Use the intended model that competitors' outcomes are independent.

$$\begin{align*}
P(\text{at least 3 not complete}) &= P(\text{3 not complete}) + P(\text{4 not complete}) \\
&= \binom{4}{3} p^1 q^3 + \binom{4}{4} p^0 q^4 \\
&= 4pq^3 + q^4
\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, or otherwise, find an expression in terms of $q$ only for the probability that a four-member team will score points.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}
P(\text{4-member scores points}) &= P(\text{at least 2 complete}) \\
&= 1 - P(\text{less than 2 complete}) \\
&= 1 - P(\text{at least 3 not complete}) \\
&= 1 - (4pq^3 + q^4) \\
\text{Substitute } p &= 1 - q: \\
&= 1 - 4(1 - q)q^3 - q^4 \\
&= 1 - (4q^3 - 4q^4) - q^4 \\
&= 1 - 4q^3 + 4q^4 - q^4 \\
&= 1 - 4q^3 + 3q^4
\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find an expression in terms of $q$ only for the probability that a two-member team will score points.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}
P(\text{2-member scores points}) &= P(\text{at least 1 completes}) \\
&= 1 - P(\text{0 complete}) \\
&= 1 - q^2
\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Hence, or otherwise, find the range of values of $q$ for which a two-member team is more likely than a four-member team to score points.

answer.worked:
For $q=0$, both team-scoring probabilities equal $1$, so the strict inequality does not hold. For $q>0$:

$$\begin{align*}
P(\text{2-member scores}) &> P(\text{4-member scores}) \\
1 - q^2 &> 1 - 4q^3 + 3q^4 \\
0 &> 3q^4 - 4q^3 + q^2 \\
3q^4 - 4q^3 + q^2 &< 0 \\
q^2(3q^2 - 4q + 1) &< 0 \\
\text{Since } q > 0\text{, } q^2 > 0 \text{, so:} \\
3q^2 - 4q + 1 &< 0 \\
(3q - 1)(q - 1) &< 0
\end{align*}$$
The roots are $q = \frac{1}{3}$ and $q = 1$.
Testing the regions gives $\frac{1}{3} < q < 1$.

content.prompt:
A game is played by throwing darts at a target.
A player can choose to throw two or three darts.
Darcy plays two games.
In Game 1, he chooses to throw two darts, and wins if he hits the target at least once.
In Game 2, he chooses to throw three darts, and wins if he hits the target at least twice.
The probability that Darcy hits the target on any throw is $p$, where $0 < p < 1$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the probability that Darcy wins Game 1 is $2p - p^2$.

answer.worked:
Use the intended model that the dart throws are independent. 

The probability of winning Game 1 (at least 1 hit in 2 throws) is $1 - P(\text{0 hits})$.
$$\begin{align*}
P(\text{Win 1}) &= 1 - (1-p)^2 \\
&= 1 - (1 - 2p + p^2) \\
&= 2p - p^2
\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that the probability that Darcy wins Game 2 is $3p^2 - 2p^3$.

answer.worked:
The probability of winning Game 2 (at least 2 hits in 3 throws) is $P(\text{2 hits}) + P(\text{3 hits})$.
$$\begin{align*}
P(\text{Win 2}) &= \binom{3}{2} p^2 (1-p) + p^3 \\
&= 3p^2(1-p) + p^3 \\
&= 3p^2 - 3p^3 + p^3 \\
&= 3p^2 - 2p^3
\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Prove that Darcy is more likely to win Game 1 than Game 2.

answer.worked:
We want to show $P(\text{Win 1}) > P(\text{Win 2})$, so consider $P(\text{Win 1}) - P(\text{Win 2})$:
$$\begin{align*}
P(\text{Win 1}) - P(\text{Win 2}) &= (2p - p^2) - (3p^2 - 2p^3) \\
&= 2p - 4p^2 + 2p^3 \\
&= 2p(1 - 2p + p^2) \\
&= 2p(1 - p)^2
\end{align*}$$
Since $0 < p < 1$, we have $2p > 0$ and $(1-p)^2 > 0$.
Thus, $2p(1-p)^2 > 0$, meaning $P(\text{Win 1}) > P(\text{Win 2})$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Find the value of $p$ for which Darcy is twice as likely to win Game 1 as he is to win Game 2.

answer.worked:
We require $P(\text{Win 1}) = 2 \times P(\text{Win 2})$.
$$\begin{align*}
2p - p^2 &= 2(3p^2 - 2p^3) \\
2p - p^2 &= 6p^2 - 4p^3 \\
4p^3 - 7p^2 + 2p &= 0 \\
p(4p^2 - 7p + 2) &= 0
\end{align*}$$
Since $p > 0$, we can divide by $p$:
$$4p^2 - 7p + 2 = 0$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{align*}
p &= \frac{7 \pm \sqrt{(-7)^2 - 4(4)(2)}}{2(4)} \\
&= \frac{7 \pm \sqrt{49 - 32}}{8} \\
&= \frac{7 \pm \sqrt{17}}{8}
\end{align*}$$
Since $\sqrt{17} \approx 4.12$, $\frac{7 + 4.12}{8} \approx 1.39 > 1$, which is outside $0 < p < 1$.
The valid solution is $p = \frac{7 - \sqrt{17}}{8}$.

content.prompt:

answer.short: Choose four wins in the first six games, then win game seven: $\binom64(\frac12)^7$.
answer.worked:
Use the intended model that the game outcomes are independent. 

For player $A$ to win the prize in exactly 7 games, they must win exactly 4 of the first 6 games, and then win the 7th game.
The probability of winning 4 of the first 6 games is given by the binomial probability $\binom{6}{4}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^4 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \binom{6}{4}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^6$.
The probability of winning the 7th game is $\frac{1}{2}$.
Multiplying these gives the overall probability:
$$\begin{align*}
P &= \binom{6}{4}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^6 \times \frac{1}{2} \\
&= \binom{6}{4}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^7
\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Write an expression for the probability of player $A$ getting the prize in at most $7$ games.

answer.worked:
Player $A$ can win the prize in 5, 6, or 7 games.
In 5 games: Wins 4 of first 4, then wins 5th $\implies \binom{4}{4}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^5$.
In 6 games: Wins 4 of first 5, then wins 6th $\implies \binom{5}{4}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^6$.
In 7 games: Wins 4 of first 6, then wins 7th $\implies \binom{6}{4}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^7$.
The probability is the sum of these mutually exclusive events:
$$\begin{align*}
P(\text{at most 7}) &= \binom{4}{4}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^5 + \binom{5}{4}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^6 + \binom{6}{4}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^7
\end{align*}$$

entries.description:
Binomial distributions
• Define a binomial random variable, X, as the number of ‘successes’ in n independent and identically distributed Bernoulli trials, with the same probability of success p in each trial, where n is a fixed finite number
• Identify contexts suitable to be modelled using binomial distributions
• Define a binomial experiment as a fixed number of Bernoulli trials
• Use the notation X ∼ Bin(n, p) to represent a binomial random variable, X, where n is the number of trials and probability of success is p
• Recognise the significance of ⁿCᵣ as the number of ways in which an outcome with r successes can occur in n trials
• Use the formula P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ to find the probability of r successes in a binomial experiment involving n trials
• Calculate the expected frequencies of the various possible outcomes from a binomial experiment, where the expected frequency of an outcome happening r times in n trials is n × P(X = r)
• Use the formulae E(X) = μ = np to find the mean, and Var(X) = np(1 − p) to find the variance when X ∼ Bin(n, p)
• Solve practical problems involving binomial distributions and binomial probabilities with and without online computational applications, excluding the normal approximation to the binomial distribution

entries.description:
Let a binomial random variable X be n repetitions of a Bernoulli trial; we multiply the Bernoulli expected value and variance by n:

Expected Value
E(X) = np

Variance & Standard Deviation
Var(X) = np(1 − p)
σ(X) = √(np(1 − p))

σ(X) is not n times the Bernoulli standard deviation.
σ(X) ≠ n√(p(1 − p)) as standard deviation does not have the linearity property.
